archetype.name: Pocket Passer (downfield-leaning)
archetype.definition: A rarely-running passer working from a very clean pocket behind a run-first offense, whose value comes from the vertical shots, while his accuracy underneath and over the middle has always lagged.

report.headline: Clean pocket, real deep ball, but accuracy and middle reads are sinking him
report.take:
Penix took over in Week 3 of a run-first Falcons offense that passes well below expectation (passRateOverExp of -6.7, 28th) and protects him better than almost anyone. He is pressured on just 10.8% of dropbacks, the lowest rate among qualifiers, and the team allows the fewest QB hits in the league. That setup should make him comfortable. Instead his season sits at -0.042 EPA per dropback (30th of 54) with a -5.27 CPOE (43rd). The volume looks fine at 216 yards a game. The efficiency underneath it is not.

The season splits into two halves. Weeks 3-7 were functional to good: positive EPA in four of five games, including clean wins at Green Bay and New Orleans. Then it fell apart. Over the last three games he has been at -0.347 EPA per dropback, a -15.3 CPOE, six interceptions, one touchdown and three losses. The Tampa game, at 8 of 24 with four picks and a 45.5% bad-throw rate, is the extreme case. Cincinnati and Kansas City were not outliers in the other direction, though. The KC game's 286 yards came with -14.6 EPA. Protection didn't cause this: his sack rate over that stretch is lower than his season mark. The problem is the throws.

The splits show where it lives. His deep ball works: +0.547 EPA on 25 attempts at 20+ air yards with no interceptions, the single best part of his game. The 10-19 yard window is the problem: 41.4% completions, a -13.2 CPOE and four of his seven interceptions. Over the middle he is at -0.312 EPA with five interceptions, while his throws to the left are clean (no picks, +9.7 total EPA). Behind-the-line throws have cost -21 EPA. That is partly scheme and supporting cast: Bijan Robinson's targets and Olamide Zaccheaus's are both deep in the red. Drake London, by contrast, has been worth +24.3 EPA on 69 targets, and he is the one reliable channel.

How much of this is new? The accuracy isn't. His CPOE was -4.4 as a rookie and -3.6 last year, ranked 51st both times, so a below-expected completion rate is simply who he is. What is new is the interception rate: 0.88 a game against 0.33 last season, while his bad-throw rate actually fell from 22.5% to 13.2%. Cleaner ball placement alongside more picks points to decisions and middle-of-the-field reads rather than raw arm misfires. Six interceptions in three games is partly bad variance, and it should cool. A low-CPOE passer in a run-first, bottom-five passing offense still has a ceiling of roughly league-average efficiency carried by the deep shots.

strengths.title: Vertical shots pay off
strengths.body: His 20+ air-yard throws have produced +0.547 EPA per attempt and +13.7 total, with zero interceptions. That is the main reason his overall numbers aren't worse. Completions are only 40% there, which is normal for that depth, and the explosive payoff carries it. On 25 attempts some regression is due, but the clean CPOE on those throws (+2.5) suggests real arm talent rather than luck.

strengths.title: Rarely pressured, rarely sacked
strengths.body: He is pressured on 10.8% of dropbacks, first among 42 qualifiers. Atlanta's line gives up the fewest QB hits in the league, and his 4.7% sack rate ranks 9th. When he is pressured he goes down a lot (33.3% pressure-to-sack, 28th), but the line rarely lets that happen. This is a team trait and should hold.

strengths.title: Drake London as a lifeline
strengths.body: London's 69 targets have returned +0.353 EPA each and +24.3 total, which is more than his whole passing game nets. When Penix feeds his WR1, the offense works. That is a stable, repeatable connection to lean on.

concerns.title: Intermediate middle is a turnover zone
concerns.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards complete at 41.4% with a -13.2 CPOE and four interceptions. Middle-of-the-field throws carry five of his seven picks at -0.312 EPA. Throws to the left have no interceptions at all, which points to reads and window choices over the middle rather than arm strength. This is the most fixable flaw, and also the one most likely to keep costing him against good zone defenses.

concerns.title: Accuracy has always lagged
concerns.body: His -5.27 CPOE ranks 43rd of 54, after ranking 51st in each of his first two seasons. This is not a slump, it is his baseline. The last three games at -15.3 exaggerate it, but even his good stretch didn't make him an accurate passer.

concerns.title: Dead weight behind the line
concerns.body: Screens and swing throws have cost -21 EPA at -0.419 per attempt. Bijan Robinson's and Zaccheaus's targets both grade deeply negative. That is largely scheme and receivers failing after the catch rather than Penix, but it drags his per-dropback numbers down every week.

trend.note: He was positive or close to it through Week 7. Then came a three-game collapse: four picks at Tampa, a flat Cincinnati game, and an empty 286 yards against Kansas City. That adds up to -0.347 EPA per dropback and six interceptions in three losses.

nextGame.headline: League's top pass defense meets a passer in free fall
nextGame.body:
Minnesota is first in defensive EPA, first in pass EPA allowed, first in QB-hit rate and first in sack rate. It allows the fewest QB fantasy points in the league (8.7 PPR a game). It also has the strongest run funnel in football: offenses pass 9.6 points less often than normal against it, and Atlanta already leans run-heavy. Expect low volume and a much heavier pass rush than Penix's clean pockets have prepared him for. His 33.3% pressure-to-sack rate becomes a real issue here. The cracks are deep throws, where Minnesota ranks only 12th, and opposing WR1s, who have hit it for 0.44 EPA a target (27th). That lines up with his two best tools: the deep ball and London. The game is in a dome, and he gets a bye week's rest.

Availability helps on both sides. Inside linebacker Blake Cashman (95% of snaps) is out, which matters for a passer whose problems live over the middle. Edge Andrew Van Ginkel is questionable and lineman Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins is out, which could soften the rush. Minnesota's offense is 30th in EPA and is missing Kyler Murray, Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings, with T.J. Hockenson also out. That points to a low-scoring game where Atlanta may not be chasing points, which keeps Penix's attempts down but also keeps him out of desperate catch-up passing.

keyMatchups.title: Minnesota's rush vs. his pocket
keyMatchups.body: Penix is almost never pressured, but Minnesota hits and sacks quarterbacks more than any defense. If its rush gets home, his high pressure-to-sack rate turns drives into punts. Van Ginkel's status is the swing.

keyMatchups.title: London against a leaky WR1 spot
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota has given up 0.44 EPA per target to opposing WR1s, among the worst in the league, even though their fantasy totals stay modest. London is Penix's most efficient target by far. Routing the passing game through him is the clearest path to a respectable day.

keyMatchups.title: Run funnel caps his volume
keyMatchups.body: Opponents run on Minnesota more than on any other defense, and Atlanta's offense already prefers the ground. With Minnesota's offense limping, game script may never force him to throw 35+ times.

nextGame.watch: Whether he stops forcing intermediate throws over the middle now that Cashman is out, or keeps feeding interceptions to the league's best pass defense.

restOfSeason.body:
The protection, the run-first structure and the London connection are stable, so the volume should sit near his season norm. The deep ball should stay a weapon, though not at quite this rate on a small sample. The six-interception, three-game spike should cool toward a more normal rate, since he threw so few picks in each of his first two seasons and his bad-throw rate has improved. Still, his intermediate and middle-of-the-field problems mean he probably settles above his old interception levels. The accuracy won't change; a below-expected CPOE has followed him every year.

The realistic expectation is a passer around 190-230 yards a game with roughly one touchdown and close to one interception. His efficiency sits at or a little below league average, propped up by explosive throws and dragged down by everything underneath. If the last three games prove to be a real decline rather than a bad run against strong defenses, his job security becomes a story. The dossier lists him as QB1, but Atlanta has started three quarterbacks this year.
swingFactors: Cleaning up intermediate and middle-of-field throws
Whether the deep-ball efficiency holds on more attempts
Game script in a run-first offense

confidence.note: Eight starts with a sharp late collapse, much of it in one four-interception game against a top defense; his career accuracy trend is consistent.
